name: The association principle and deterministic psychology
plain_explanation: The theory that mental life -- ideas, words, and their connections -- is built up entirely out of habitual associations, so that, in principle, a person's thoughts and reactions could be explained the way a scientist explains any other natural process.
precise_definition: Hartley's and Bentham's doctrine that association of ideas with ideas, and of ideas with language, is the basic mechanism of mental life, aimed at a fully deterministic account of mental occurrences; Russell treats it as essentially the same doctrine, in purely mental terms, as Pavlov's later, physiologically grounded conditioned reflex.
why_it_mattered: It gave Bentham's legal and political reforms a scientific-sounding psychological foundation: if human reactions are lawful and predictable, a code of laws could in principle be engineered to make men virtuous automatically.
historical_origin: Emphasised by Hartley in 1749; earlier, Locke had recognized association of ideas only as a source of trivial errors.
examples: Pavlov's conditioned reflex, which Russell treats as the modern, physiological descendant of the association of ideas
objections: Russell notes that Bentham and his followers, like some behaviourists after Pavlov, 'exaggerated the extent of the field' to which the principle validly applies
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates twentieth-century behaviourism's materialist recasting of the same basic idea via the conditioned reflex.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Underwrote Bentham's confidence that legislation could reshape human character.
